Predicting functions of uncharacterised genes from co-essentiality

An explainer of an AI-run project. Not verified by a human.

The method: predicting functions of uncharacterised genes from co-essentiality, with honest confidence

In one sentence: to propose functions for human genes that databases call "uncharacterised", the method takes a gene list frozen in advance plus DepMap CRISPR knockout screens, and returns for each gene one predicted Gene Ontology (GO) function, a calibrated probability that curators will later confirm it, and labels that say when not to trust it.

In three sentences: each gene's 25 strongest co-essential partners (genes whose knockout hurts the same cancer cell lines) are found with a published scoring tool, the GO term carried by the most strongly linked partners becomes the prediction, and genes whose partner list does not reproduce in two halves of the cell lines are flagged and kept off the shortlist (a prediction is still written for them). How much to trust a prediction is learned from the future, not the past: a calibration model is fitted on 809 genes that were uncharacterised in 2018 and gained experimental annotations afterwards, after removing annotations from papers that themselves used DepMap. The top predictions are then checked against independent interaction and localisation data, and against the literature by blinded judges who also see three decoy statements per gene.

Key numbers (honest version)

Measure Value
Genes pre-registered as uncharacterised 4,924 of 19,296 (4,271 measurable in DepMap)
Genes with a usable, reproducible signal 646 pass the rule (13%); allowing for false passes, at least ~322 (6.5%) carry real signal [post-review estimate, untested assumption]
Accuracy on genes annotated after 2018 (top term right) 3.0% (95% CI 1.8–4.3%), vs 0.5% for matched genes; no better than the older GLS score (2.3%) and far below homology (21.8%)
Highest calibrated probability for any gene 0.141, so no gene reached the pre-set confidence tiers (0.3, 0.5)
Expected confirmed predictions ~4.9 (2.2–8.1) over 2,583 calibrated genes; 30.5 if every gene were later annotated [post-review]. About 82% of this comes from genes that fail the usable-signal rule: over the 269 assessable genes it is ~0.9 (5.5 if every gene were annotated) [derived for this explainer, not in the manuscript]
Blinded literature check of the top 40 18/40 supported vs 3/120 decoys (p = 0.0002); 16/40 on the GO term alone
Novelty of the top 40 31/40 already had a published function; 34/40 had a link in earlier catalogues [post-review]

How it differs from the standard approach

The standard approach to predicting function from CRISPR screens is guilt by association. Score every pair of genes by how similar their knockout profiles are across cell lines (a plain correlation, or GLS, a correlation after correcting for related cell lines; Wainberg 2021, doi:10.1038/s41588-021-00840-z). Then give an uncharacterised gene the function that is over-represented among its top partners. Accuracy is usually measured by leave-one-out: hide a well-studied gene's annotations, predict them from its neighbours, and count hits. Success is often illustrated with a few genes whose function was first proposed from co-essentiality and later confirmed.

This method keeps the guilt-by-association core and changes what surrounds it.

Standard approach This method Why it matters here (evidence)
Which genes Chosen during analysis Frozen list, defined from annotation databases before any gene–gene score (Step 1) Results cannot be tuned to the gene list; the list is checkable by hash
Pair score Correlation or GLS The published zavg_BEF tool, used unchanged (Step 2) Required by the brief. On function prediction it tied GLS (+0.006, CI −0.005 to +0.017)
When to abstain Rarely Every gene gets a top term, but genes whose partner list does not reproduce in split halves, or that are not expressed, are flagged and kept off the shortlist (Step 3) 0% accuracy in the two weakest fifths of hold-out genes by partner strength (the gate itself was not tested on the hold-out)
Artefacts Often ignored Same-chromosome-arm genes and paralogues removed from partner lists (Step 4) Removes CRISPR-cutting and copy-number look-alikes (Lazar 2024); shown on synthetic data, no measurable effect on the hold-out (3.3% without vs 3.0% with)
How accuracy is measured Leave-one-out on known genes Genes uncharacterised in 2018 and annotated since, with DepMap-citing annotations removed (Step 5) Leave-one-out gave 13.9% top-term accuracy; the 2018 hold-out gave 3.0%
Confidence A rank or a p-value A calibrated probability, p_cal, fitted on the hold-out (Step 5) A calibration fitted on known genes predicted 8.9% where 3.1% was observed
Literature check Searches with the prediction in mind Evidence collected blind, judged against three decoys per gene (Step 7) Judges' false-support rate is measurable (3/120); a language model "recognised" 43 of 59 published functions from the name alone

Why this matters. Each change exists because a looser version overstated what co-essentiality can do. Leave-one-out on well-studied genes made the method look about five times more accurate than it was on genuinely new annotations. Most of the celebrated co-essentiality success stories turned out to be circular as validation, because their new GO annotations cite papers that used DepMap (18 of 19 targets for SLC25A51, 14 of 15 for FIRRM). The pipeline writes a top term for 4,137 genes, but at most about 650 carry a reproducible signal, so the usable-signal flag decides which genes may enter the shortlist. The result is a smaller, less exciting, but honest claim: co-essentiality gives specific, low-accuracy predictions for a minority of strongly dependent genes. How each change came about is told in JOURNEY.md.

The pipeline at a glance

Steps 3 to 6 attach labels to every scorable gene rather than discarding genes: a prediction is written for all 4,137 genes with a reportable term, but only expressed, assessable genes with a calibrated probability can enter the top 40. PNG version: figures/pipeline.png.

The seven steps

Each step says what it does, why it is needed, what goes wrong without it, which turning point in the project's history shaped it, where the idea came from, and where the code is. Terms are defined in the glossary.

Step 1. Pre-register the uncharacterised genes

What it does. Before any gene-to-gene co-essentiality score exists, it defines "uncharacterised" from annotation databases only, applies the rule to all 19,296 human protein-coding genes, and freezes the resulting list with a cryptographic hash. A gene is in the list U if:

  • D1: it has no informative GO biological-process or molecular-function annotation backed by experimental or curator evidence (codes EXP, IDA, IPI, IMP, IGI, IEP, TAS, IC). Generic terms such as "protein binding" do not count;
  • and either D2, a UniProt annotation score of 2 or less (out of 5), or D3, at most 10 "focused" PubMed papers (papers that list at most 10 human genes) or IDG target class "Tdark" (the Illuminating the Druggable Genome class for proteins with almost no literature or functional annotation).

This gives 4,924 genes, of which 4,271 have a DepMap profile the tool can score. An independent agent rebuilt the list from the raw files with its own code and got the same genes. Every script that touches pairwise DepMap data first calls a gate that refuses to run unless the frozen hash and git tag match.

Why it is needed. If the gene list is chosen after seeing the network, it can drift towards genes where the network looks informative, and every later count is biased. The same rule (D1) also defines the hold-out genes of Step 5 at the 2018 GO release, so the hold-out resembles the target genes by construction.

What goes wrong without it. The benefit is that results are checkable, not a measured gain in accuracy: a chronology audit confirmed that no pairwise output predates the freeze. The step also exposed a cost of database definitions. In a random 50 of the 4,924 genes, a literature audit found that 42% (95% CI 29–56%) already had an experimentally established function ("curation lag"). Genes that entered through the literature-attention route (D3: few focused papers or Tdark) without a low UniProt score were N1 (function established) in 56% of cases (19/34), against 13% (2/16) for genes with a low UniProt score [post-review]. Counting only "focused" papers makes protein-complex subunits, which are usually described in multi-subunit papers, look unstudied (288 listed genes are Complex Portal subunits). No gene was removed after the freeze; the caveat travels with every result.

Shaped by: TP1, with the entry-route analysis from TP8. Ideas from: knownness measures and research-attention bias (Stoeger 2018, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.2006643; Haynes 2018, doi:10.1038/s41598-018-19333-x; Unknome, Rocha 2023, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.3002222; IDG Tdark, Oprea 2018, doi:10.1038/nrd.2018.14); the UniProt score ≤ 2 threshold follows Wainberg 2021. Code: scripts/02_gene_knownness_table.py, scripts/03_build_preregistration.py, src/knownness.py (d1, d2, d3, combine_u), src/gate.py (check); outputs in preregistration/.

Step 2. Score co-essentiality with the published tool (read-only)

What it does. It runs the co-essentiality tool zavg_BEF (github.com/cancergenetics/ai-hackathon-Coessentiality, commit 3c684c9) unchanged, at its published settings, on DepMap 26Q3 (1,361 cell lines). The tool gives every gene pair one score from three views of the knockout profiles, each put on a common scale against random gene pairs and averaged:

  • F, how similar the two cleaned profiles are (cleaning removes the 20 strongest screen-wide patterns, a regularised form of the GLS whitening of Wainberg 2021);
  • B, how much the two genes' top-44 partner lists overlap;
  • E, how close the two genes sit in a 512-dimensional map of the whole partner network.

Higher means the two genes are needed by the same cell lines beyond what screen-wide patterns explain. The tool, its design and its own validation are explained in its repository (docs/explainer/METHOD.md); this project did not modify or tune it.

Why it is needed. The partner list is the only evidence the method uses. Every later step reads the full gene × gene score matrix (18k × 18k) or its top-ranked rows.

What goes wrong without it. Not much, for this purpose. Before use, the project reproduced the tool's published benchmark (average precision 0.3451 against 0.345 published), matched its GLS and Pearson baselines to within 3 × 10⁻⁷, and passed 14 of 14 sign and orientation checks. On the 2018 hold-out, zavg_BEF predicted functions no better than GLS (+0.006, 95% CI −0.005 to +0.017) or plain Pearson correlation (+0.002). The tool's large lead in finding protein-complex pairs did not become a lead in predicting GO function. Believed, not tested: the bottleneck is the step from partners to a GO term, and the scarcity of strongly dependent new genes.

Shaped by: no turning point; the brief fixed the tool (JOURNEY.md). Ideas from: the tool (zavg_BEF), building on co-essentiality as evidence of shared function (Pan 2018, doi:10.1016/j.cels.2018.04.011; Kim 2019, doi:10.26508/lsa.201800278; Wainberg 2021). Code: scripts/00_get_tool.sh, scripts/10_full_matrix.py, scripts/11_reproduce_tool.py, scripts/12_sanity_checks.py, scripts/16_baseline_rows.py, src/coess_matrix.py (fit_model, write_tool_matrices); the tool itself in external/coessentiality/ (read-only).

Step 3. Decide whether the gene has a usable signal

What it does. It asks whether a gene's partner list is stable enough to read, and labels the gene "assessable" or not. It does not stop the later steps: every scorable gene still gets a top term (Step 4) and, if in calibration support, a p_cal (Step 5); the label decides whether the gene can enter the shortlist (Step 6). The cell lines are split into two halves five times (balanced by tissue and screening library, with lines from the same patient kept together), and the tool is refitted on each half. Each half gives a top-25 partner list, built with the exclusions of Step 4.

  • R(g), the split-half reproducibility: the overlap of the two half-lists, as a fraction of 25, averaged over the five splits.
  • Null: the same overlap computed between the gene's half-A list and the half-B lists of 200 matched genes (genes with similar mean effect, spread and missing data). The empirical p is (1 + number of matched genes with overlap ≥ R) / 201.
  • Assessable means p < 0.05 and the gene is expressed (log2(TPM+1) ≥ 1, TPM being transcripts per million, in at least 10% of DepMap models, or in at least half the lines of one lineage). Non-expressed genes are scored anyway, as a negative control.

Why it is needed. Many uncharacterised genes are barely expressed or never essential, so their knockout profiles are flat noise and their "top partners" are arbitrary. Even among expressed genes, about half are never hits in any CRISPR screen, often because a paralogue buffers their loss (Dede 2020, doi:10.1186/s13059-020-02173-2). Such genes should be labelled "no usable signal" rather than given a confident-looking shortlist place.

What goes wrong without it. Not tested directly: the hold-out was never split by this gate, so there is no accuracy figure for assessable versus non-assessable genes. The evidence is indirect. On the hold-out, accuracy was 0 in the two weakest fifths of genes by partner strength (mean score of the 25 neighbours) and 11.7% (6.7–17.4%) in the strongest fifth; the gate correlates with partner strength but is not the same thing. Only 2 of 516 chemosensory/epidermal-family genes passed. The step has a known weakness: non-expressed control genes passed the reproducibility test 13% of the time (27% among those with any dependency), against a nominal 5%. Applying those false-pass rates back, the 646 assessable calls exceed the null expectation by about 241 (168–306), which at full power implies at least ~322 genes (6.5%, 242–388) with real signal, under the untested assumption that the controls' false-pass rates apply to expressed genes [post-review]. (The manuscript quotes 243 and 324 for the 635 calls under the frozen list's expression column; see DISCREPANCIES B13.) In the calibration model of Step 5, R(g) received zero weight once partner strength was known; so assessability works as a gate, not as a confidence score. The gate matters for how headline numbers are read: about 82% of the summed p_cal comes from genes that fail it (Step 5).

Shaped by: TP3, with the null-adjusted reading from TP8. Ideas from: the round-1 statistics reviewer's demand for a true cross-gene null rather than a quantile; matching on profile covariates (Rubin 1980; Stuart 2010). Code: scripts/13_matched_lists.py, scripts/14_splithalf.py, scripts/15_assessability.py, src/splithalf.py (split_halves, half_neighbours, reproducibility, assessable, expression_strata), src/predictor.py (match_genes).

Step 4. Assign a candidate function

What it does. It turns the partner list into one GO term.

  1. Neighbours N(g): the 25 highest-scoring partners, after removing genes outside the tool's well-measured background, genes on the same chromosome arm and Ensembl paralogues.
  2. Vocabulary V2: GO biological-process and molecular-function terms with 5–200 annotated genes, where a gene counts as a member only through experimental or curator evidence (propagated up the GO hierarchy). An interaction-based annotation (evidence IPI) of a neighbour is dropped if it names the query gene, so the gene cannot vote for itself through a neighbour.
  3. Term score: S(g, t) = sum of max(zavg_BEF, 0) over neighbours annotated to term t. Each such neighbour is a supporting partner.
  4. Reportable: a term needs at least 2 supporting partners. The prediction is the top reportable term (ties broken by GO identifier; the most specific term among the top five is reported alongside).

Why it is needed. Partners are evidence about a module; curators annotate GO terms. Some rule has to turn many partners with many annotations into one testable claim. The same-arm and paralogue exclusions exist because CRISPR cutting can delete large parts of a chromosome arm, and copy-number changes move neighbouring genes together, so genes near each other can look co-essential for reasons unrelated to function (Lazar 2024, doi:10.1038/s41588-024-01758-y); paralogues can share guide RNAs or compensate for each other.

What goes wrong without it.

  • Choice of ranker. Three rankers were declared before any data: R1 (the summed score above), R2 (hypergeometric over-representation) and R3 (comparison with matched genes). A fixed rule chose R1 on 2,519 well-studied genes: mean reciprocal rank 0.169, against 0.140, 0.111 and 0.073 for frequency alone. Shuffling annotations among genes collapsed top-term accuracy from 13.9% to 1.5%, so the signal comes from the network, not from term popularity.
  • Broad terms. The worry that a sum favours large terms was partly right: R1's top terms had a median of about 131 annotated genes, against 35 for R2. This is the multifunctionality bias of Gillis & Pavlidis (2011, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0017258).
  • Ties. The top score was tied in 401 of 820 hold-out genes, usually between a term and its parent. Reversing the tie order changed 393 labels but left accuracy almost unchanged (3.2% instead of 3.0%).
  • Exclusions. In the project's synthetic test, genes sharing a "chromosome-arm" artefact called their artefact term first 100% of the time without the exclusion and 0% with it. On the real hold-out, dropping the exclusions changed accuracy little (3.3% instead of 3.0%), so the guard costs nothing measurable; it can, however, discard a true partner (see TARBP2 in the worked example).
  • "≥ 2 partners" barely filters. On synthetic null data every gene still had a reportable term. Confidence has to come from Step 5.

Shaped by: TP4. Ideas from: neighbour-voting guilt by association (Pan 2018; Wainberg 2021); multifunctionality and edge-dependence critiques (Gillis & Pavlidis 2011; 2012, doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002444); chromosome-arm proximity artefacts (Lazar 2024). Code: scripts/30_loo_ranker_choice.py, scripts/31_label_shuffle.py, scripts/40_u_predictions.py, src/neighbours.py (top_k), src/vocab.py (build_v2, IPI rule), src/predictor.py (term_scores, score_table, top_terms, most_specific).

Step 5. Calibrate confidence on a temporal hold-out

What it does. It measures accuracy, and learns a probability, on genes whose function was discovered after the annotations used to predict it.

  • Hold-out H: freeze GO at 2 July 2018. Take genes that met rule D1 then, had at most 10 focused papers by then, and gained experimental GO terms since: 820 genes, 5,965 new (gene, term) targets. Predict each gene's function from its neighbours' 2018 annotations and score the top term against the terms it received later. (The co-essentiality network is from 2026 data, so only the annotations are rolled back.)
  • Circularity filter: every paper behind a target annotation was searched in Europe PMC full text for DepMap or co-essentiality terms; flagged annotations were removed (106 targets; 809 genes remain).
  • Comparators: a frequency-only ranking ("prior-only"), a matched-gene null (the same predictor run from five genes with similar profiles), GLS, Pearson, homology (the gene's own 2018 electronic and phylogenetic annotations) and protein-interaction transfer from hu.MAP 3.0.
  • Calibration: a logistic regression, with signs fixed in advance, of "top term later confirmed" on four covariates (mean score of the 25 neighbours, R(g), the share of neighbours with any annotation, and the size of the top term) plus the term's family. It is fitted on the 775 hold-out genes with a prediction and checked by cross-fitting over clusters of genes that share papers. Applied to U, it gives p_cal, but only for genes whose covariates lie inside the hold-out's 5th–95th percentiles and whose term family has at least 30 hold-out genes ("in support").

The specification was written to LOOKS.md 31 minutes before the hold-out was opened, once.

Why it is needed. Leave-one-out tests well-studied, multifunctional genes, which are easy to predict from network position alone and unlike the genes the method is for. A temporal split reproduces the real situation: predict now, be checked later.

What goes wrong without it.

  • Leave-one-out gave top-term accuracy 13.9%; the hold-out gave 3.0%. Part of this gap reflects different genes, not only leakage (open question; DISCREPANCIES C4).
  • A calibration fitted on leave-one-out genes predicted a mean probability of 0.089 on the hold-out, where 0.031 was observed.
  • Without the circularity filter, the named success stories would count as validation. The filter removed only 1.8% of targets overall (accuracy 3.2% → 3.0%), but most targets of exactly those genes. Of 14 named controls, only TMEM242 ranked its true term first, and only in the descriptive case series (worked example).
  • p_cal is conditional. Every hold-out gene did gain annotation, so p_cal estimates P(top term confirmed | the gene is annotated later). Only 16% of eligible 2018 genes gained annotation in about 8 years, so the expected number of confirmations among the 2,583 calibrated genes is about 4.9 (2.2–8.1), not 30.5 [post-review].
  • Most of that comes from genes without a usable signal. Of the 30.5, only 5.49 (2.81–8.64) comes from the 269 expressed, assessable genes in support (results/ledger/pcal_summary.json); the other 82% comes from genes that fail Step 3. Rescaled by the same 16.1% annotation rate (775/4,822), the 269 assessable genes are expected to yield about 0.9 (roughly 0.45–1.4, ignoring uncertainty in the rate) confirmed top terms [derived for this explainer; the manuscript does not state it; DISCREPANCIES B19].
  • The model rests on 24 correct calls. Out-of-fold calibration slope 0.82 (0.51–1.13); c-statistic 0.86 (the chance that a randomly chosen correct call gets a higher probability than a randomly chosen wrong one); Brier skill only 2% (the Brier score, the mean squared error of the probabilities, is only 2% better than always predicting the base rate): not detectably off, but thin. Simpler models calibrate as well but share only 7–14 of the top 40 genes with it [post-review].

Shaped by: TP2, TP5 and TP8. Ideas from: the CAFA time-split design (Radivojac 2013, doi:10.1038/nmeth.2340; Zhou 2019, doi:10.1186/s13059-019-1835-8); logistic calibration and its checks (Cox 1958; Van Calster 2019, doi:10.1186/s12916-019-1466-7); cluster bootstrap (Field & Welsh 2007); intersection–union test (Berger 1982). Code: scripts/04_holdout_sizing.py, scripts/05_circularity_query.py, scripts/32_holdout_core.py, scripts/33_holdout_secondary.py, scripts/34_calibration_fit.py, scripts/41_pcal.py, src/calibration.py (MonotoneLogistic, cross_fit, support_mask, p_cal), src/metrics.py, src/ledger.py (pcal_from_model, support_category).

Step 6. Add orthogonal evidence and prioritise

What it does. It ranks candidates and attaches independent evidence and warnings to each.

  • Orthogonal evidence: data that never saw DepMap, in five classes: physical interaction (BioPlex, OpenCell, BioGRID low-throughput, STRING experiments; Human Cell Map), protein co-abundance (ProteomeHD, CCLE proteomics), localisation (Human Protein Atlas), Perturb-seq and AlphaFold2 pair models. Sources were admitted only if they recovered known complexes before any prediction existed (11 of 12 pair sources passed). For a prediction, each source tests whether the gene is closer to the predicted term's members than 1,000 degree-matched random member sets; p-values are combined within a class (Simes) and across classes (Holm, α = 0.05).
  • Artefact flags: overlapping loci, copy-number co-amplification and hub-driven scores; a prediction with flags on half or more of its supporting partners is excluded from the top.
  • Prioritisation: the design promised tiers (Tier A: p_cal ≥ 0.5 plus orthogonal support; Tier B: p_cal ≥ 0.3). No gene reached either, so a pre-written "low-yield" branch applied: the top 40 is the 40 highest p_cal values among expressed, assessable, in-support genes (269), after artefact exclusions and one contradiction (245 remain), with mitochondrial calls capped at 6 of the top 20.
  • Labels, not demotions: top-40-only checks (refit without the most dependent lineage, replication in DEMETER2 RNAi data, TP53 dependence) are shown next to each gene.
  • A separate list (S20): the 20 strongest predictions that cannot be calibrated (machinery families with fewer than 30 hold-out genes, or signals beyond the hold-out's range), kept apart from the calibrated top 40.

Why it is needed. p_cal is one number from one data type. Independent data can catch artefacts, and a reader needs to know which predictions rest on hubs, neighbouring loci or a single tissue.

What goes wrong without it, and what went wrong with it. The checks were never validated on known positives before they could demote genes, and they did not separate signal from noise. Orthogonal support passed 32% of real predictions, 28% of matched-gene predictions and 22% of decoy-term predictions (247 each); in the top 40, 62.5% vs 47.5% vs 25%. The robustness checks failed 221 of 269 candidates, 182 of 204 of them on RNAi replication. Using them as demotions (an agent's "clean-first" fill) would have produced a top 40 sharing only 20 genes with the p_cal order. Without the separate S20 list, the best-established co-essentiality signals (mitochondria, DNA repair, ribosome, nuclear RNA, centrosome) would be invisible, because the calibration's support rule excludes them; judges later supported 19 of those 20, all with earlier catalogue links (Rahman 2021, doi:10.15252/msb.202010013, documents this mitochondrial dominance).

Shaped by: TP6. Ideas from: independent evidence classes, each source admitted only if it recovered 2,538 known complexes not derived from hu.MAP (design choice, DESIGN §5); Simes 1986 and Holm 1979 for combining tests; mitochondrial bias in screens (Rahman 2021). Code: scripts/20_source_admission.py, scripts/42_artefact_flags.py, scripts/43_orthogonal_support.py, scripts/44_tiers_top40.py, scripts/46_top40_primary.py, src/support.py (source_test, support_test, simes, holm), src/orthogonal.py, src/ledger.py (exclusion_43, tier_of, fill_top).

Step 7. Check the literature blind

What it does. It asks whether published evidence supports each top prediction, in a way that measures how easily "supported" is said.

  1. Recall probe: before anything else, a language model without tools says what it knows about each gene. This measures how much a model "already knows".
  2. Blind literature screen: a separate agent with no access to predictions or co-essentiality output searches the literature and writes an evidence table with verbatim quotes, and classes each gene N1 (function established), N2 (partial) or N3 (none).
  3. Statements and decoys: each prediction becomes a script-written statement (GO term plus a module label). It is shown with three decoys, the top terms of other genes matched on term family and size, in random order. Gene names are redacted from the evidence; a leak check found none.
  4. Judge validation: on 10 hold-out genes with known answers, the judges had to support at least 7 of 10 real statements and at most 3 of 30 decoys. They scored 9/10 and 1/30.
  5. Judging: two independent judges score every statement +1 (supported), 0 (not addressed) or −1 (contradicted); an adjudicator resolves disagreements. The test is a one-sided sign-flip test of real minus mean decoy score over the top 40.

Why it is needed. An agent that knows the prediction and then searches will find support. A model may also simply remember gene functions: the recall probe "recognised" 43 of 59 genes with an established function. Decoys turn literature support into a test with a measurable false-support rate.

What goes wrong without it. Without decoys there is no way to tell real support from leniency; with them, judges supported 18 of 40 real statements against 3 of 120 decoys (p = 0.0002). Without the novelty classes the 18 would read as discoveries; 16 of the 18 were N1 genes whose function was already published. The judging rule itself mattered: the judge prompt credited a match to "the stated process or module", a choice that was not logged before judging. Counting the GO term only gives 16/40 (p = 7 × 10⁻⁴) [logged retrospectively]. Agreement between the two judges (κ = 0.975) shows that two instances of one model agree, not that they are right.

Shaped by: TP7, with the scoring-rule and novelty corrections from TP8. Ideas from: blinded assessment with decoys (design choice of this project, DESIGN §6.2–6.4); Cohen's κ (Cohen 1960); symbol hygiene for literature agents (previous symbols and aliases). Code: scripts/50_m7_prep.py, scripts/51_judge_packets.py, scripts/52_judge_analysis.py, src/redact.py, src/metrics.py (sign_flip_test, cohens_kappa); agent prompts verbatim in docs/AGENT_PROMPTS.md.

Worked example: ANKRD52 through all seven steps

ANKRD52 came out rank 1 of the primary top 40. Its predicted function, microRNA-mediated gene silencing, had already been published, so the reader can watch the method recover an answer that is known to be right. Every number below was recomputed by worked_example.py, which calls the pipeline's own functions; 159 of 159 values matched the committed results (details and all tables: worked_example_notes.md, worked_example_output/). The notes number their sections 0–7 by pipeline stage; the mapping to the seven method steps is given in each panel title below.

Step 1 · Pre-registration: why ANKRD52 counts as "uncharacterised"

ANKRD52 has three experimental GO rows, all "protein binding" (evidence IPI). That term is generic, so it has 0 informative terms: D1 is true. Its UniProt annotation score is 3, so D2 is false. It has 6 focused papers (62 in total), so D3 is true. It entered U through D1 + D3.

This is a curation-lag case. A 2017 study (PMID 28114302) showed that the ANKRD52–PPP6C phosphatase removes phosphates from AGO2 and that this cycle is needed for microRNA silencing. GO never recorded it with an experimental code. The blind literature agent later classed ANKRD52 as N1 (function established), and co-essentiality catalogues had already linked it to the microRNA machinery (Kim 2019; Wainberg 2021). The example is a validation, not a discovery.

Step 2 · Co-essentiality scores

ANKRD52 has a value in all 1,361 cell lines (mean gene effect −0.243, SD 0.231; 12.4% of lines below −0.5): a weak, selective dependency. The method uses the pattern of these values. Across all genes, ANKRD52's zavg_BEF scores have median −0.09 and 99.9th percentile 5.4; its strongest partners score far above that.

rank partner zavg_BEF z_B z_E z_F
1 AGO2 25.76 43.28 20.59 13.41
2 XPO5 24.40 42.90 20.19 10.11
3 DICER1 23.69 41.51 19.84 9.70
8 PPP6C 13.62 20.85 11.76 8.25

Step 3 · Usable signal

Over five split halves, ANKRD52's two top-25 lists shared 10, 10, 13, 13 and 13 genes: R = 0.472. AGO2, XPO5, DICER1, DROSHA, DGCR8, TNRC6A/B, CNOT9 and PPP6R1 were shared in every split. Against its 200 matched genes the mean null overlap was 0.0037 (maximum 0.20), so none reached R: p = 1/201 = 0.005. ANKRD52 is expressed (median log2(TPM+1) 3.94), so it is assessable. Context: only 646 of 4,924 genes pass, and 13% of non-expressed controls pass the p-value part.

Step 4 · Candidate function

Neighbours. Two same-arm genes (ANKRD52 is on 12q) and three paralogues were removed. One of them, TARBP2 (score 13.42, would have ranked 9th), is a Dicer cofactor: the artefact guard threw away a true partner. The 25th neighbour scores 4.52; the mean over the 25, 10.68, is reused in Step 5.

Terms. 22 of 25 neighbours carry at least one annotation; 238 terms get S > 0 and 45 are reportable. Ranks 3 and 4 are tied (a parent and child term with the same five supporting partners), a live case of the tie problem of Step 4.

rank GO term S supporting partners
1 regulatory ncRNA-mediated gene silencing (GO:0031047) 158.11 8
2 post-transcriptional gene silencing 115.69 6
3 regulatory ncRNA-mediated post-transcriptional gene silencing 92.00 5
4 miRNA-mediated post-transcriptional gene silencing 92.00 5
5 miRNA processing 91.87 4

S = 25.76 + 24.40 + 23.69 + 22.37 + 21.00 + 20.05 + 16.27 + 4.57 = 158.11 (AGO2, XPO5, DICER1, DROSHA, TNRC6A, DGCR8, TNRC6B, DDX6). ANKRD52's biochemical home, the PP6 phosphatase (PPP6C, PPP6R1, PPP6R3 and PTPA are all neighbours), ranks only 37th (phosphoprotein phosphatase activity, S = 24.9), because few PP6 members carry experimental GO terms. The GO vote follows the best-annotated partners.

Step 5 · Calibrated probability

covariate ANKRD52 hold-out 5th–95th percentile coefficient
mean score of the 25 neighbours 10.68 3.33–10.99 +0.285
R(g) 0.472 0–0.546 0 (shrunk to its bound)
annotated-neighbour share, as a percentile 0.859 0.075–0.894 +1.704
top-term size, as a percentile 0.172 0.049–0.950 0 (shrunk)

logit = −6.3155 + 0.28504 × 10.682 + 1.70378 × 0.8591 = −1.807, so p_cal = 0.141: the highest of the 2,583 calibrated genes, yet below Tier B (0.30). On the hold-out, genes in the top probability decile (mean 0.170) were confirmed 11.5% of the time (6.2–20.5%). Read p_cal as "about a one-in-seven chance that this exact GO term is experimentally annotated within about 8 years, if the gene is annotated at all".

Step 6 · Orthogonal evidence and rank

Tested against the 62 genes annotated to the predicted term: physical interaction p = 0.565 (its physical edges go to PP6 subunits and TNRC6B), co-abundance p = 0.028, localisation p = 0.021, Perturb-seq and structure not measured. Holm needs the smallest class p ≤ 0.05/3 = 0.0167, so no class is called "supports", and there is no contradiction. The same test gave a matched gene (MTA2) co-abundance and localisation support, and gave a decoy term nothing. ANKRD52 passed the top-40-only checks that could be run (lineage leave-out, no expression coupling, no TP53 effect; RNAi not measured). It is rank 1 of 245 eligible genes.

Step 7 · Blind literature check

The literature agent found 11 items (7 functional) and classed ANKRD52 N1. In its judging packet (J071) the judges saw four statements with the gene name redacted:

slot statement real? judge 1 judge 2
A modulation of chemical synaptic transmission decoy 0 0
B deacylase activity decoy 0 0
C regulatory ncRNA-mediated gene silencing; RISC complex real +1 +1
D dicarboxylic acid metabolic process decoy 0 0

Both judges cited the AGO2-dephosphorylation evidence. Real minus mean decoy score: d = 1. Over the top 40, 18 genes were supported like this, most of them, like ANKRD52, rediscoveries.

Hold-out control · TMEM242 (how the method was validated)

TMEM242 shows the hold-out logic. In 2018 it had no informative GO term. Its 25 neighbours are dominated by ATP synthase subunits (ATP5F1A/B/C/D/E, ATP5PB/PD/PF/PO and others) plus TMEM70, OXA1L and STOML2 (mean score 13.05, R = 0.67). In 2021 one paper (PMID 33753518, not flagged as DepMap-derived) gave it five terms, including mitochondrion organization and three ATP-synthase-assembly terms.

analysis term window top term from 2018 annotations later received?
named-control case series (descriptive) 2–300 genes mitochondrion organization (S = 272, 18 partners) yes, rank 1 of 77
primary hold-out endpoint (pre-registered) 5–200 genes generation of precursor metabolites and energy no; the in-window later terms ranked 49 and 50

Stated plainly: TMEM242 is a miss on the pre-registered primary endpoint and a hit only in the descriptive case series. The term it received has 204 annotated genes, just above the 200-gene ceiling, and the specific assembly terms had too few annotated neighbours in 2018. Its out-of-fold p_cal was 0.28. It is the only one of 14 named controls whose true term ranked first, and that only under the wider window.

Pseudocode and where each step lives in the code

# Step 1  (before the freeze; annotation data only)
U = {g in HGNC protein-coding : D1(g, GO_now) and (D2(g) or D3(g))}       # 4,924 genes
freeze(U, design, config) -> FREEZE.sha256 + git tag; gate.check() guards every later pairwise script

# Step 2  (tool, read-only)
Z = zavg_BEF(DepMap_26Q3)                       # gene x gene score; mean of z-scored F, B, E

# Step 3
for g in scorable(U):
    N_A[s], N_B[s] = top25(tool(half_A[s]), g), top25(tool(half_B[s]), g)   for s in 0..4
    R[g]  = mean_s |N_A[s] ∩ N_B[s]| / 25
    R0[m] = mean_s |N_A[s](g) ∩ N_B[s](m)| / 25   for 200 matched genes m
    p[g]  = (1 + #{m : R0[m] >= R[g]}) / 201
    assessable[g] = p[g] < 0.05 and expressed[g]

# Step 4
N(g) = top 25 of Z[g, :] excluding self, non-background, same chromosome arm, paralogues
S(g, t) = sum_{j in N(g), j annotated to t} max(Z[g, j], 0)             # V2 terms, 5-200 genes, IPI rule
top_term(g) = argmax_t S(g, t) over terms with >= 2 supporting partners  # ties: ascending GO id

# Step 5  (one look at H)
H = genes with D1 at GO 2018-07-02, <= 10 focused papers, new experimental terms since; drop DepMap-citing annotations
rerun Steps 3-4 for H with 2018 annotations; hit[g] = top_term(g) in new_terms(g)
model = sign-constrained logistic(hit ~ mean Z of N(g) + R + coverage_pct + size_pct + family), cluster cross-fitted
p_cal(g in U) = model(g) if covariates within H's 5th-95th percentiles and family has >= 30 H genes else none

# Step 6
support(g) = Holm over classes(Simes over sources(empirical p vs 1,000 degree-matched member sets))
pool  = U genes that are expressed, assessable, in support, without artefact exclusion or contradiction
top40 = pool sorted by p_cal (tiers A/B first if any; mitochondrial <= 6 of top 20); checks attached as labels

# Step 7
for g in top40 (+ S20, extra30, 10 validation genes): evidence(g) = blind_literature_agent(g)  # N1/N2/N3
packet(g) = shuffle([statement(top_term(g))] + 3 decoys); redact names; judges J1, J2 (+ adjudicator)
test: one-sided sign-flip on d(g) = score(real) - mean(score(decoys))

1 Pre-register 02_gene_knownness_table.py, 03_build_preregistration.py knownness.py, gate.py preregistration/uncharacterised_genes.tsv, FREEZE.sha256
2 Score 00_get_tool.sh, 10_full_matrix.py, 11_reproduce_tool.py, 12_sanity_checks.py, 16_baseline_rows.py coess_matrix.py (+ tool in external/coessentiality/) data/derived/matrices/zavg_full/, results/verification/
3 Usable signal 13_matched_lists.py, 14_splithalf.py, 15_assessability.py splithalf.py, predictor.py (match_genes) results/assessability/assessability_U.tsv

5 Calibrate 04_holdout_sizing.py, 05_circularity_query.py, 32_holdout_core.py, 33_holdout_secondary.py, 34_calibration_fit.py, 41_pcal.py calibration.py, metrics.py, ledger.py results/holdout_eval/, results/calibration/model_H.json, results/ledger/u_pcal.tsv

Results and how strong the evidence is

What was evaluated. Four claims, fixed in the frozen design: how many pre-registered genes carry a usable signal (C1); top-term accuracy on the 2018 hold-out against nulls (C2, the primary test); calibrated predictions for the pre-registered genes (C3); and blinded literature support for the top 40 (C4). Labels: pre-specified (frozen design), deviation (a logged change), exploratory (post hoc, before review), post-review (requested by referee agents after the first manuscript draft; no frozen rule changed).

Ranker choice (2,519 known genes) R2, R3, frequency only MRR 0.169 vs 0.140, 0.111, 0.073 Pre-specified rule
