How strong is the evidence? The primary test (C2) is the strongest result: specified 31 minutes before a single look, re-derived by an independent agent, robust in all 10 split-half networks and every circularity variant. But the effect is small (24 correct genes out of 809), and the comparison that matters most for a user, homology, is lost sevenfold. The literature result (C4) is significant but easy: decoys are other genes' terms, so a gene with any literature can win on topic alone, and judges were two instances of one model. The calibration is formally adequate but rests on 24 events, and the top-40 ranking it produces is fragile. Nothing was validated at the bench, and no human has checked any result.

Limitations, assumptions and when not to use it

Assumptions.

  • GO experimental annotation is a fair proxy for "function established". It is not: 42% of a random sample of "uncharacterised" genes already had published function.
  • Genes annotated after 2018 behave like today's uncharacterised genes. The hold-out genes have stronger signal than U (reweighting to U drops accuracy from 3.0% to 1.2%), and p_cal is conditional on later annotation.
  • The 2026 DepMap network carries no post-2018 knowledge about the hold-out genes. Only annotations were rolled back; the tool's settings were tuned on hu.MAP 3.0, built after 2018. Parity with untuned Pearson bounds this leak but does not measure it.
  • Non-expressed genes estimate the false-pass rate of Step 3 for expressed genes (untested).

What was not validated.

  • No prediction was tested experimentally; the ten candidate reports propose experiments only.
  • The orthogonal-support rule and the top-40 robustness checks were never validated on known positives.
  • Within-gene decoys (the gene's own lower-ranked terms) were not run, so the judging does not show that the top term beats the gene's other candidates.
  • Judges' validity rests on 10 validation genes and the decoy rate; heterogeneous judges (other models, human curators) were not used.
  • Novelty against Pan 2018, FIREWORKS and Perturb-seq clusters could not be checked; prior-knowledge counts are lower bounds.
  • Temperatures and seeds of model calls were not recorded; the agent-run log has one row.

When not to use it.

  • As a general annotator. Use homology or interaction-based transfer first; co-essentiality adds a few distinct correct calls (+0.6 points) where homology is silent.
  • For genes without a usable signal (not assessable, not expressed, chemosensory or epidermal families): the method about 87% of the pre-registered genes fail the usable-signal rule. Their predictions are still written and some carry a p_cal, but they are flagged and should not be read as evidence.
  • Reading p_cal as the chance that the biology is right. It is the chance that this exact GO term is curated with experimental evidence, given that the gene is annotated at all.
  • Expecting novelty. Check earlier co-essentiality catalogues (Wainberg 2021; Kim 2019) before calling a prediction new.
  • For machinery genes (mitochondria, ribosome, DNA repair, nuclear RNA, centrosome): they have no calibrated probability; use the separate, uncalibrated S20-style list and treat it as descriptive.
  • Without checking neighbouring-gene and paralogue artefacts if the exclusions in Step 4 are removed.

Glossary

  • AP (average precision). The area under a precision–recall curve; the tool's own benchmark measure for finding co-complex pairs.
  • Assessable. A gene whose top-25 partner list reproduces across split halves (p < 0.05 against matched genes) and that is expressed. See Step 3.
  • Background (BG). Genes with less than 10% missing DepMap values (17,525 genes); only these can be neighbours.
  • Brier score, Brier skill. The mean squared error of predicted probabilities; skill is the fractional improvement over always predicting the base rate.
  • c-statistic. The chance that a randomly chosen correct call gets a higher predicted probability than a randomly chosen wrong one (0.5 = no discrimination).
  • Calibration, calibrated. Probabilities are calibrated if, among predictions given 0.1, about 10% come true.
  • Calibration support ("in support"). A gene whose covariates lie within the hold-out's 5th–95th percentiles and whose term family has at least 30 hold-out genes; only these get a p_cal (2,583 genes).
  • Chronos gene effect. DepMap's estimate of how much knocking out a gene slows a cell line's growth: 0 no effect, about −1 a typical essential gene (Dempster 2021, doi:10.1186/s13059-021-02540-7).
  • Circularity filter. Removal of hold-out target annotations whose supporting papers mention DepMap or co-essentiality in full text.
  • Clean negative. A gene not expressed (log2(TPM+1) < 0.5) in at least 95% of cell lines; used as a negative control.
  • Cluster bootstrap. Confidence intervals from resampling clusters of genes that share supporting papers, so that related genes are not counted as independent.
  • Co-essentiality. Two genes are co-essential when their knockout profiles across cell lines rise and fall together, which often means shared function.
  • Coverage. The share of a gene's 25 neighbours with at least one annotation; enters calibration as a percentile.
  • Curation lag. A function is published but not (yet) recorded in GO with experimental evidence.
  • D1, D2, D3. The three knownness criteria of Step 1.
  • Decoy. Another gene's predicted term, matched on family and size, shown to judges (or tested for orthogonal support) as a negative control.
  • DepMap. The Cancer Dependency Map; release 26Q3 has 1,361 cell lines and 18,434 genes.
  • Evidence codes. GO annotation provenance: experimental (EXP, IDA, IPI, IMP, IGI, IEP), curator/author (TAS, IC), electronic (IEA), similarity (ISS), phylogenetic (IBA) and others.
  • Expressed. log2(TPM+1) ≥ 1 in at least 10% of DepMap models or in at least half the lines of one lineage.
  • extra30. 30 further genes from the top-40 pool, six per p_cal fifth, judged as a secondary set.
  • GLS. Generalised least squares correlation: a profile correlation after removing the correlation between related cell lines (Wainberg 2021).
  • GO; BP, MF, CC. Gene Ontology; biological process, molecular function, cellular component.
  • H (hold-out). 820 genes uncharacterised in GO on 2 July 2018 that gained experimental terms since (809 after the circularity filter).
  • Homology baseline. Ranking the gene's own 2018 electronic, similarity and phylogenetic GO terms.
  • hu.MAP 3.0. A protein-complex atlas from proteomics (Fischer 2025, doi:10.1038/s44320-025-00121-5); used as a comparator, never as support.
  • Intersection–union test. The primary test passes only if the method beats both nulls.
  • IPI rule. An interaction-based annotation of a neighbour is ignored if its partner field names the query gene.
  • κ (kappa). Cohen's chance-corrected agreement between two judges.
  • Leave-one-out (LOO). Hide a known gene's annotations and predict them from its neighbours; here used only to choose the ranker.
  • Matched gene. A gene with similar mean effect, spread and missing data, used as a null.
  • MRR. Mean reciprocal rank of the first correct term.
  • N(g), neighbours. The 25 highest-scoring partners of gene g after exclusions.
  • N1, N2, N3. Literature classes: function established, partial evidence, none.
  • Orthogonal evidence. Data independent of DepMap: physical interaction (P), co-abundance (A), localisation (L), Perturb-seq (G), structure (S).
  • p_cal. Calibrated probability that a gene's top GO term will be confirmed with experimental evidence within about 8 years, given that the gene gains new experimental annotation.
  • Paralogue. A gene related by duplication (Ensembl); excluded from neighbour lists.
  • Precision@1. The fraction of genes whose single top term was later received.
  • Prior-only. A ranking by term frequency alone; a null comparator.
  • R(g), R0. Split-half reproducibility of a gene's partner list, and its null analogue against matched genes.
  • R1, R2, R3. Candidate term rankers: summed score, hypergeometric p, matched-gene empirical p. R1 was chosen.
  • Reportable. A term with at least 2 supporting partners.
  • S(g, t), term score. Sum of positive zavg_BEF scores of neighbours annotated to term t.
  • S20. The 20 strongest predictions without a p_cal, judged separately.
  • Same-arm exclusion. Removal of neighbours on the same chromosome arm, against CRISPR-cutting and copy-number artefacts.
  • Scorable. Has a DepMap profile the tool can score (4,271 of the 4,924 genes).
  • Sign-flip test. A permutation test of whether real-minus-decoy differences are centred above zero.
  • Simes, Holm. Methods to combine p-values within a class and to correct across classes.
  • Split halves. Two random halves of the cell lines, balanced by lineage and screening library.
  • Supporting partner. A neighbour annotated to the term, with a positive score.
  • Σp_cal. Sum of p_cal over genes: the expected number of confirmations.
  • Tdark. The Illuminating the Druggable Genome (IDG) class for proteins with almost no literature or annotation.
  • Temporal hold-out. Predict from annotations frozen at an earlier date and score against annotations added later.
  • Tier A / B. Pre-set confidence tiers (p_cal ≥ 0.5 plus orthogonal support / p_cal ≥ 0.3); empty in this study.
  • TPM. Transcripts per million, a unit of gene expression; log2(TPM+1) is its log scale.
  • Top-K mean zavg. The mean zavg_BEF of a gene's 25 neighbours; the main calibration covariate.
  • U. The 4,924 pre-registered uncharacterised genes.
  • V2; V1, V1′. Prediction vocabulary (GO BP + MF); descriptive module labels (GO complexes; plus Complex Portal and MitoCarta).
  • zavg_BEF; z_B, z_E, z_F. The tool's co-essentiality score, the mean of its three z-scored views (shared neighbours, graph embedding, first-order similarity).

How we got here

The main point: the method in METHOD.md looks the way it does because one rule was applied again and again: fix the rule before seeing the answer, then test it on genes whose function was discovered after 2018. Each of its seven steps exists because a check showed that a looser version would have overstated what co-essentiality can do. Three consequences shaped the final result:

  1. The gene list came first. "Uncharacterised" was defined from annotation databases and the 4,924-gene list was frozen by a hash before any gene–gene score was computed (TP1). This kept the study honest. A later audit showed that the definition also admitted many genes whose function is already published, which became a finding of its own ("curation lag").
  2. Confidence was measured on the future. Accuracy and calibration come from 809 genes that were uncharacterised in 2018 and gained experimental annotation since (TP2, TP5). Co-essentiality's top GO term was right for 3.0% of them, which is above chance (0.5%), no better than an older co-essentiality method (GLS), and far below the gene's own 2018 electronic annotations (21.8%).
  3. Every count was cut down by its control. Only a few hundred genes carry a usable signal (TP3), no gene reached the pre-set confidence tiers (TP6), and blinded literature judges mostly confirmed functions that were already published or already predicted (TP7). Referee agents forced the final framing, an honest evaluation rather than a discovery list, at the very end (TP8).

Step 2 (scoring co-essentiality) has no turning point of its own. The brief fixed the tool, and the agents only checked that it ran correctly on DepMap (it reproduced its published benchmark, 0.3451 against 0.345).

The project ran from 19:39 on 29 October to 10:26 on 30 October 2026 (UTC; publication clean-up followed at 11:39–11:52). A principal-investigator agent ("the PI", Claude Opus 5.5) designed the study and made the decisions. Sub-agents (Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5) did the literature work, data handling, code, reviews, blinded roles, reports and red-teams. The PI estimates that it used about 60 of them; this cannot be checked, because the run log meant to record every agent (results/agent_runs.tsv) has one row. A human wrote the brief and supplied the DepMap files. All times below are git commit times. They show when work was recorded, not when it started, and several commits bundle work done earlier.

Words used below

  • DepMap, Chronos gene effect. DepMap (release 26Q3: 1,361 cancer cell lines, 18,434 genes) screens cell lines with genome-wide CRISPR knockout libraries. For each gene and line, the Chronos model (Dempster 2021, doi:10.1186/s13059-021-02540-7) estimates how much knocking the gene out slows growth: 0 means no effect, −1 is the median effect of common essential genes.
  • Co-essentiality. Two genes are co-essential when their gene-effect profiles across cell lines rise and fall together, which often means they work in the same complex or pathway (Wainberg 2021, doi:10.1038/s41588-021-00840-z; Pan 2018, doi:10.1016/j.cels.2018.04.011). A gene's neighbours are its 25 most co-essential partners.
  • zavg_BEF, GLS. zavg_BEF is the co-essentiality score this project had to use: an AI-built, label-free score that averages three similarity views of whitened profiles (the tool: github.com/cancergenetics/ai-hackathon-Coessentiality, commit 3c684c9; its own explainer is in that repository's docs/explainer/). GLS is the earlier method of Wainberg 2021, which "whitens" the profiles (removes the correlation between related cell lines) before correlating them.
  • GO term, BP/MF/CC. Gene Ontology terms describe a gene's biological process (BP), molecular function (MF) or cellular component (CC). Terms form a hierarchy, so a gene annotated to a specific term also counts for its ancestors.
  • Evidence codes. Each GO annotation records how it was obtained: experimental (EXP, IDA, IPI, IMP, IGI, IEP), curator or author statements (TAS, IC), high-throughput (HTP and relatives), phylogenetic (IBA), similarity (ISS) or purely electronic (IEA). "Experimental annotation" below means the first two groups.
  • Temporal hold-out. Freeze the annotations at an earlier date (here GO of 2 July 2018), predict, and score against annotations added later. This is the design of the CAFA function-prediction challenges (Radivojac 2013, doi:10.1038/nmeth.2340). Here the hold-out set has 820 genes (809 after the circularity filter).
  • Precision@1. The fraction of genes whose single top-ranked GO term is one they later received.
  • Calibration, p_cal. A score is calibrated if, among predictions given probability 0.1, about 10% turn out right. p_cal is the calibrated probability that a gene's top term will be confirmed, from a logistic model fitted on the hold-out.
  • Assessable, split-half. The cell lines are split into two halves (balanced by lineage and screening library). A gene is assessable when its neighbour list from one half overlaps its list from the other half more than expected by chance, and the gene is expressed. Otherwise its prediction is still written but flagged, and it cannot enter the shortlist.
  • Decoy. A plausible but wrong statement (another gene's prediction of similar type and size) shown to literature judges alongside the real one, so that their support rate on decoys measures how easily they say "supported".
  • Curation lag. A gene's function is published, but the databases have not recorded it yet (or do not record it in the fields our definition used).
  • N1/N2/N3. A blind literature agent's verdict on a gene: N1 function established, N2 partial or indirect evidence, N3 nothing functional published.
11. Defining "uncharacterised" before looking (20:06–21:00, revisited 21:16 and 08:15)4,924 genes hash-frozen; later 42% found already published

In short. Uncharacterised = no experimental GO process/function annotation AND (UniProt annotation score <= 2 OR <= 10 focused PubMed papers OR IDG Tdark); 4,924 genes frozen by hash before any gene-gene score. A later audit found 42% already had published function, mostly among genes entering via the literature-attention route (few focused papers or Tdark) without a low UniProt score (56% vs 13%).

Situation. The brief required a pre-registered list of uncharacterised genes before any analysis of the co-essentiality network. Nothing in the brief said what "uncharacterised" means.

Options considered. The literature review (LITERATURE.md §3) compared five measures of how well a gene is known:

  • experimental GO process/function annotations;
  • the UniProt annotation score (a 1–5 measure of how much an entry contains; Wainberg 2021 called genes with score ≤ 2 uncharacterised);
  • PubMed paper counts, after Stoeger 2018 (doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.2006643), who showed that research attention is concentrated and self-reinforcing;
  • IDG "Tdark" status, the Illuminating the Druggable Genome class for proteins with almost no literature or annotation (Oprea 2018, doi:10.1038/nrd.2018.14);
  • Unknome "knownness" (Rocha 2023, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.3002222), a family-level evidence-weighted GO score.

It also flagged that annotation is unequal and biased (Haynes 2018, doi:10.1038/s41598-018-19333-x).

What decided it. The review recommended combining them: no experimental GO process/function annotation, and either a low UniProt score or low literature attention. The experimental-GO part could be computed for any archived GO release, which the hold-out in TP2 needed. The final rule (DESIGN.md §1) was:

no experimental GO BP/MF annotation and (UniProt annotation score ≤ 2 or ≤ 10 "focused" PubMed papers — papers listing ≤ 10 human genes — or IDG Tdark).

The list (4,924 genes; 4,271 scorable in DepMap) was built from annotation files only, re-derived exactly by an independent agent with its own code, and frozen with a SHA-256 hash and git tags (afed1dd, 21:00). Scripts that compute gene pairs refuse to run unless the hash matches, and the tool's precomputed genome-wide predictions were hidden until then (preregistration/PROVENANCE.md).

What happened next. Sixteen minutes after the freeze, an audit agent with no access to network outputs searched the literature for a random 50 of the genes (b2b3a53). It found that 21/50 (42%, 95% CI 29–56%) already had an experimentally established function (results/audit/curation_lag_audit.md). Thirteen of these were published since 2021, so GO had not yet caught up. Eight had evidence 7–17 years old that was never turned into GO annotations. Following the pre-registration, no gene was removed from the list. Only after manuscript review did an analysis split this by entry route (b39691d, results/revision/SUMMARY.md §A1). Genes that entered through the literature-attention route (D3: few focused papers or Tdark) without a low UniProt score (3,819 of 4,924) were N1 in 19/34 cases (56%), against 2/16 (13%) for genes with a low UniProt score. The reason is mechanical: counting only "focused" papers makes complex subunits, which are usually characterised in multi-subunit papers, look unstudied. 288 listed genes are curated Complex Portal subunits, and 1,261 have the maximum UniProt score of 5.

Outcome. Step 1 as frozen, plus the census and the curation-lag caveat that every later result carries.

Where: f1cb5c3 (LITERATURE.md, DESIGN v1), afed1dd (freeze), b2b3a53 (audit), b39691d (entry routes); DESIGN.md §1, preregistration/.

Shaped Method step 1 →

22. How to validate a function prediction (20:06–21:00)820 hold-out genes; DepMap-citing annotations removed

In short. Primary validation = CAFA-style temporal hold-out (genes uncharacterised in GO 2018-07, annotated since), with prior-only and matched-gene nulls and a full-text circularity filter that removes annotations from papers that used DepMap. Leave-one-out on known genes was demoted to choosing the ranker.

Situation. The usual way to test guilt-by-association predictors is leave-one-out: hide a known gene's annotations, predict them from its neighbours, and score. Gillis & Pavlidis showed why this flatters predictors. Multifunctional, well-annotated genes are easy to "predict" from network degree alone (2011, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0017258), and performance often rests on a handful of edges (2012, doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002444). Leave-one-out also tests well-studied genes, which are not like the uncharacterised genes the project cares about.

Options considered.

  • leave-one-out on known genes;
  • a set of literature "success stories", in which a function was first proposed from co-essentiality and later confirmed (SPRING1, SLC25A51, FIRRM, CCDC32, TEDC1/2 and others; LITERATURE.md §2);
  • a CAFA-style temporal hold-out (Radivojac 2013; Zhou 2019, doi:10.1186/s13059-019-1835-8).

What decided it. The temporal hold-out was already the primary test in the first design, as recommended by the literature review (f1cb5c3, LITERATURE.md §4.1). The first review round (six role-specific reviewer agents, 3e6b162) made it stricter. The PI's own account credits that round with the hold-out itself; the record shows that the review round hardened it (see DISCREPANCIES.md).

  • Hold-out genes: genes that met the "uncharacterised" rule in GO 2018-07 with ≤ 10 focused papers by then, and gained experimental BP/MF terms since. That gives 820 genes and 5,965 new (gene, term) targets.
  • Two nulls to beat: "prior-only" (always guess the most frequent terms) and a matched-gene null (the same predictor run from genes with similar essentiality profiles).
  • A circularity filter. Every paper behind a target annotation was searched in Europe PMC full text for DepMap, co-essentiality or co-dependency terms. Flagged annotations were removed, because they may themselves come from co-essentiality.
  • Leave-one-out was kept only to choose a ranker (TP4).

Outcome. The circularity filter removed only 1.8% of hold-out targets (106/5,965), and precision@1 changed from 0.032 to 0.030. But it removed most targets of exactly the celebrated success stories: SLC25A51 18/19, FIRRM 14/15, CCDC32 4/5 (results/holdout/circularity_summary.md). SPRING1, TEDC1/2 and POU2AF2/3 were not in the hold-out at all, because their new terms fell outside the 5–200-gene term window. Only TMEM242 of 14 named controls ranked its true term first. So the success stories became a descriptive case series, not evidence. In hindsight, the choice of hold-out mattered a great deal: leave-one-out gave precision@1 0.139, the hold-out 0.030 (part of this gap reflects different genes, not only leakage). This turning point produced Step 5.

Where: f1cb5c3, 3e6b162, reviews/round1_statistics.md items 8–13, reviews/round1_disposition.md, DESIGN.md §3.2.

Shaped Method step 5 →

33. Which genes can the method say anything about? (20:18–21:55, revisited 08:15)646 assessable (13%); excess over null about 241

In short. A gene is flagged assessable if its neighbour list reproduces across split halves of the cell lines better than for 200 matched genes, and the gene is expressed. 646 of 4,924 pass; non-expressed control genes pass the reproducibility test 13% of the time, so calls exceed the null expectation by only about 241 (at least ~322 genes with real signal).

Situation. Many uncharacterised genes are barely expressed or never essential, so their CRISPR profiles are flat noise and their "neighbours" are arbitrary; even among expressed genes, about half are never CRISPR hits, often because a paralogue buffers them (LITERATURE.md §1.4, citing Dede 2020, doi:10.1186/s13059-020-02173-2). The design needed a rule, fixed in advance, that flags such genes as having no usable signal rather than promoting a confident wrong prediction.

Options considered. The first design called a gene assessable when the overlap of its neighbour lists between two random halves of the cell lines reached the 95th percentile of overlaps for matched genes. Two round-1 reviewers objected. The statistics reviewer wrote that matched genes' own reproducibility "includes real signal, so the current rule keeps the top 5% of each essentiality stratum. That is a quantile, not a null" (reviews/round1_statistics.md item 11). The external-PI reviewer proposed a profile-informativeness filter or a permutation null.

What decided it. The adopted rule (DESIGN.md §4.2) compares a gene's split-half overlap with its own list against the overlap between its list and those of 200 matched genes (a cross-gene null). It splits lines five times, stratified by lineage × library with patients kept together, and also requires the gene to be expressed. Non-expressed genes were scored anyway as a negative control. On a synthetic toy dataset the null genes passed 1.7% of the time.

Outcome. At 21:55 (0e76668) 646 of 4,924 genes (13.1%) were assessable. Only 2 of 516 chemosensory/epidermal-family genes and 43 of 742 tandem-cluster genes passed. The negative control showed the catch. Clean non-expressed genes passed the reproducibility part 13% of the time, and 27% of those with any dependency, against the nominal 5% (results/assessability/summary.md). Until manuscript review this was reported with the sentence "the expression requirement carries the specificity". The statistics referee showed that this does not follow (TP8). Applying the control's false-call rates to the expressed genes leaves an excess of about 241 calls (168–306) over the null expectation among the 646, which implies at least about 322 genes (6.5%) with real signal under an untested assumption (243 and 324 on the 635 calls of the frozen expression column, the basis the manuscript quotes) (b39691d, results/revision/SUMMARY.md §A6, results/revision/a10_assessability_excess_and_implied.tsv). This turning point produced Step 3 and its caveat.

Where: 3e6b162, 0e76668, b39691d; reviews/round1_external_PI.md item 2.

Shaped Method step 3 →

44. Turning neighbours into a function call (22:19; tie found 23:07)MRR 0.169 vs 0.140 vs 0.111; 401/820 top ties

In short. Three pre-declared rankers compared once on 3,000 sampled known genes (2,519 with a target) by a fixed rule; the summed partner score won and collapsed under label shuffling. An independent verifier later found tied top scores in 401 of 820 hold-out genes.

Situation. Each gene has 25 neighbours, many of them annotated to many GO terms. Which single term should be the prediction?

Options considered. The round-1 statistics reviewer worried that a raw sum would favour large, generic terms and hub genes. The design therefore pre-declared three rankers (DESIGN.md §3.1):

  • R1 summed score: for each term, add the positive co-essentiality z-scores of the neighbours annotated to it;
  • R2 hypergeometric p: is the term over-represented among the neighbours?
  • R3 matched-gene empirical p: does this gene's score for the term beat the scores of 500 matched genes?

A fixed rule chose between them: the highest mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of the first correct term on 3,000 sampled known genes outside the uncharacterised list and the hold-out (2,519 kept a target after circular annotations were removed), with near-ties (|ΔMRR| < 0.005) going to R3, then R1. Only terms with ≥ 2 supporting neighbours count.

What decided it. The simplest ranker won clearly. MRR was 0.169 for R1, 0.140 for R2, 0.111 for R3 and 0.073 for prior-only. R1 also won in every circularity sensitivity analysis (results/calibration/loo_ranker_choice.md, 47631ed). Shuffling the annotations among genes collapsed precision@1 from 0.139 to 0.015, so the signal comes from the network, not from term frequencies (results/calibration/label_shuffle.md). The reviewers' worry was partly right: R1's top terms are broad (median 131 annotated genes, against 35 for R2).

Outcome. Step 4. The independent agent that re-derived the hold-out result (809/809 per-gene agreement, 8e7e47f) found a gap: R1's top score was tied in 401 of 820 hold-out genes, usually between a term and its parent, which have the same supporting neighbours. The design had fixed ties only for R3. The implementation broke ties by ascending GO identifier. Reversing that order changes 393 top-term labels but leaves precision@1 almost unchanged (0.032 instead of 0.030). The tie rule is now logged (DEVIATIONS.md), and the reports also give the most specific term among the top five.

Where: 47631ed, 8e7e47f, verify/holdout_verification.md.

Shaped Method step 4 →

55. The single look at the hold-out (22:19 → 22:50)precision@1 0.030 vs 0.005 null; homology 0.218

In short. Specification logged 31 min before the hold-out was opened once. Primary test passed (0.030 vs 0.000 prior-only and 0.005 matched-gene null), no better than GLS, far below the gene's own 2018 electronic/phylogenetic annotations (0.218). Calibration not detectably off, but based on 24 correct calls.

Situation. With the ranker chosen, the hold-out could be opened. Any design choice made after seeing its outcome would contaminate it.

What was done. The PI wrote the ranker and the full calibration specification into LOOKS.md (fa21808, 22:19). The calibration model is a sign-constrained logistic regression of "top term correct" on the neighbours' mean score, split-half reproducibility, the share of annotated neighbours, term size and term family, cross-fitted over clusters. Because neighbour-sharing linked 63.5% of hold-out genes into one cluster, a fallback to clustering by shared papers was also logged before the look. Thirty-one minutes later an agent opened the hold-out once (aa381fc). A further agent re-derived the primary result independently (8e7e47f).

What it showed (results/holdout_eval/SUMMARY.md):

  • The primary test passed, modestly. Precision@1 was 0.030 (95% CI 0.018–0.043), against 0.000 for prior-only and 0.005 for the matched-gene null. That is 24 correct genes out of 809. The result held in all 10 split-half networks and every circularity sensitivity. The freeze-time power simulation had assumed null precision of 0.05–0.15, far above the 0.000–0.005 observed.
  • No better than GLS. zavg_BEF − GLS was +0.006 (−0.005 to +0.017), and Pearson correlation was within 0.002. The tool's large lead over GLS on its own co-complex benchmark did not carry over to function prediction.
  • Far below homology. Simply ranking the gene's own 2018 electronic and phylogenetic (IEA/ISS/IBA) terms gave 0.218. Protein-interaction transfer from hu.MAP 3.0 gave 0.049.
  • Signal only where dependency is strong. Precision@1 was 0.117 in the strongest-signal fifth of genes and 0 in the two weakest. For complex membership (GO CC complexes, 77 genes) it reached 0.182. Reweighted to resemble the uncharacterised genes, it fell to 0.012.
  • Calibration not detectably off. The out-of-fold slope was 0.82 (0.51–1.13) and the c-statistic 0.86 (the chance that a correct call is ranked above a wrong one), so p_cal was permitted under the pre-registered branch. The model rests on only 24 correct calls, a point the referees later made central (TP8). A calibration fitted on leave-one-out genes would have predicted 0.089 on the hold-out against 0.031 observed.

Outcome. Step 5 and the paper's framing: co-essentiality is a calibrated, specific but weak signal for a minority of strongly dependent genes, not a general annotator. A logged exploratory look (70864b2) showed it is complementary to homology: 15 of its 24 hits were missed by homology. As a deployable rule ("homology if it predicts, else co-essentiality") it adds +0.006 (0.218 → 0.224; post-review, b39691d).

Where: fa21808, aa381fc, 8e7e47f, 70864b2; LOOKS.md.

Shaped Method step 5 →

66. Nobody reaches the confidence tiers (04:55)max p_cal 0.141 vs Tier A 0.5

In short. Highest calibrated probability 0.141, so the pre-registered low-yield branch applied. The PI ranked the top 40 by p_cal (overriding an agent's clean-first fill) and added a separate, uncalibrated list of 20 strong-signal genes from machinery families outside calibration support.

Situation. The design (DESIGN.md §6.1) promised tiers. Tier A needed p_cal ≥ 0.5 plus orthogonal support, Tier B p_cal ≥ 0.3. If fewer than 10 genes reached Tier A, a pre-written "low-yield branch" applied: lead the paper with the census and accuracy results, and fill the top 40 by tier, then p_cal.

What the predictions showed (c4eadf5, results/ledger/M6_SUMMARY.md). 4,137 genes received a top term. The highest p_cal among the 2,583 genes inside the calibration's support was 0.141, so no gene reached either tier and the low-yield branch applied. Two further problems surfaced:

  • Robustness checks failed almost everything. The top-40-only checks (lineage leave-out, RNAi replication in DEMETER2, TP53 dependence) failed 221 of 269 candidates. RNAi non-replication alone accounted for 182/204. The checks had never been tried on known positives.
  • Orthogonal support barely separated anything. Physical, co-abundance, localisation and perturbation data passed 32% of real predictions, 28% of matched-gene predictions and 22% of decoys (n = 247 each).

Options considered and decision. The implementing agent filled the top 40 "clean first": genes passing every check, even with p_cal near 0, ranked above flagged genes with p_cal ≥ 0.06. It also kept two genes that carried built-in exclusions. The PI overrode this. Without tiers, the demotions are inert (they only cap a gene at Tier B), so the frozen fill key reduces to p_cal, and the clean-first list became a sensitivity analysis (DEVIATIONS.md, row "§6.1 top-40 fill"). The PI also saw that the calibration's support rule excluded every prediction in five "machinery" families (mitochondria, DNA repair, ribosome, nuclear RNA, centrosome), each with fewer than 30 hold-out genes. It also excluded the strongest signals, which lay beyond the hold-out's 95th percentile. Those are where co-essentiality is best established (Rahman 2021, doi:10.15252/msb.202010013, documents the dominance of mitochondrial modules). Thirty seconds after the predictions were committed, and before any literature step, the PI defined a separate, uncalibrated list of 20 strong-signal genes (6a95b71), judged and reported apart from the primary 40.

Outcome. Step 6 as it now stands: rank by p_cal, show failed checks as labels rather than demotions, and keep the uncalibrated strong-signal list separate.

Where: c4eadf5, 6a95b71; reviews/retro_M7.md §1 items 2–3.

Shaped Method step 6 →

77. Blinded literature judging with decoys (05:05–05:38; caveat logged 07:47)18/40 real vs 3/120 decoys supported (p = 0.0002)

In short. Literature agents blind to predictions wrote evidence tables; judges scored each real prediction against three decoys, after passing a validation on known genes (9/10 real vs 1/30 decoys). 18/40 real vs 3/120 decoys supported; 16/40 when module-label matches are not credited.

Situation. The brief asked for a literature check of the best predictions. An agent that knows the prediction and then searches the literature will tend to find support. A language model may also simply remember gene functions: a closed-book probe "recognised" 52 of 90 candidate genes.

What was done (pre-specified in DESIGN.md §6.2–6.4, prompts in docs/AGENT_PROMPTS.md):

  1. Blind literature agents (Sonnet) saw only gene identifiers. They wrote evidence tables with verbatim quotes from retrieved papers and assigned N1/N2/N3, for 100 genes (10c3219).
  2. Script-templated statements. Each gene got its real predicted term and module label plus three decoys (other genes' predictions from the same family and similar size, with no ancestor or descendant overlap), in random order. Gene names were redacted from the evidence. A leak check found zero leaks (991c5f1).
  3. Judge validation first. On 10 hold-out genes, where the "real" statement was a known true term, the judges supported 9/10 real against 1/30 decoys, which passed the pre-set bar of ≥ 7/10 and ≤ 3/30 (1eb08ea, adjudicated in 020b0ed).
  4. Main judging. Two judges and an adjudicator; agreement κ = 0.975.

Outcome (020b0ed, results/m7/judge/analysis_main.md):

  • Primary top 40: 18/40 real predictions supported against 3/120 decoys (exact sign-flip p = 0.0002).
  • The 20 uncalibrated strong-signal genes: 19/20.
  • 30 lower-p_cal genes: 1/30. Support tracks p_cal.

But 16 of the 18 supported genes were N1, already published. Manuscript review then found that the judge instructions credited a match to "the stated process or module". That operational choice existed only in the agents' prompt and had not been logged before judging. Counting term matches only gives 16/40 (p = 7×10⁻⁴); the change was logged retrospectively (acdad5a). The referee also noted that κ near 1 between two instances of one model measures reproducibility, not validity; validity rests on the decoys and the validation set. This turning point produced Step 7.

Where: 3776d47 → 020b0ed, acdad5a; reviews/ms_round1_referee_stats.md referee items M4 and S1.

Shaped Method step 7 →

88. Review-driven reframing (07:47–10:26)about 5 expected confirmations; 1 of 10 reports new

In short. Referee agents showed that p_cal is conditional on a gene being annotated later (unconditional expected confirmations about 5, not 30.5), that the census counted null calls, and that 9 of 10 report genes already had a published co-essential link (3 an explicit Wainberg 2021 prediction). Only PLEKHH3 had no prior.

Situation. Manuscript v1 (07:36) said co-essentiality "recovers function for curation-lag genes" and gave about 30.5 expected confirmations among calibrated predictions. Two referee agents (domain and statistics), plus number, reference and reproducibility auditors, reviewed it (3f3a65b). Both referees recommended major revision.

What the referees found (reviews/ms_round1_referee_domain.md, reviews/ms_round1_referee_stats.md):

  • p_cal is conditional. The hold-out contains only genes that did gain annotation (820 of 5,051 eligible, 16%). So p_cal estimates P(top term confirmed | the gene is annotated later), not the chance of confirmation. Rescaled by the 2018 cohort's annotation rate, the expected number of confirmations drops from 30.5 to about 4.9 (2.2–8.1).
  • The census counted null calls. See TP3: the 646 assessable genes include roughly 400 expected false calls.
  • The definition admits known complex subunits. 20 of the top 40 had the maximum UniProt score and 13 were Complex Portal subunits. This led to the entry-route analysis in TP1.
  • Novelty was never checked against earlier catalogues. After the review, 34/40 top genes had a link with at least one of their top-10 partners in earlier co-essentiality or interaction resources. For the ten deep-dive reports, 9/10 genes already had a published co-essential relationship with their partners (Wainberg 2021 modules or pairs; Kim 2019, doi:10.26508/lsa.201800278). Three of them, INAFM1, CCDC71L and C5orf34, were explicit function predictions in Wainberg 2021's Supplementary Data 3 (2e2e9c2, results/revision/report_novelty_corrections.md). Only PLEKHH3, a proposed brake on PI3K/AKT signalling, has no prior in any resource checked.
  • "Calibration was adequate" overstated a model fitted on 24 events, with one family coefficient at −11.9 because that family had 0 hits in 111 genes.

What changed. Post-review analyses were run as logged, exploratory looks (b39691d). The manuscript was rewritten (v2, 0cde51b) and reviewed again: both referees recommended minor revision, and every post-review number was independently recomputed (ed9a54b). The final version came at 10:26 (a739f06). No pre-specified result changed; the interpretation did. The title now reads "modest accuracy, narrow reach and many already-published functions". This turning point produced no new step, but it fixed the caveats on Steps 1, 3, 5 and 7.

Where: 3f3a65b, b39691d, 2e2e9c2, 0cde51b, ed9a54b, a739f06; reviews/ms_round1_response.md, reviews/ms_round2_response.md.

Fixed the caveats in the Method →

The research process

Who did what.

  • The PI agent (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote the design from the literature review, all decision notes in RESEARCH_TREE.md, the hold-out specification and the low-yield interpretations (TP6), and committed everything with explicit paths. Agents did not commit.
  • Sub-agents did the literature review, data download and checksums, the pipeline code (160 tests), 11 design reviews in two rounds plus two disposition checks, independent re-derivations (the gene list, the hold-out and the hold-out result), three chronology audits, the curation-lag audit, recall probes, blind literature agents, judges and an adjudicator, ten report writers with red-team reviewers, manuscript referees, number and reference checkers, and three retrospectives. Model assignments for the blinded roles are in docs/AGENT_PROMPTS.md. The total (about 60 by the PI's estimate) is not logged.
  • The human wrote the brief (PROMPT.md) and had the DepMap 26Q3 files on the machine; the PI found them, and their checksums matched the tool's own data list, so the tool ran on exactly the release it was built for. According to the PI's account, the human otherwise asked status questions, resumed the run after a usage-limit pause (08:16–09:16, 379827f), and gave publication instructions (16de609 onwards). The record contains no human scientific direction; this account cannot be checked against a transcript.

Where exploration was productive.

  • Mechanisms instead of promises. The hash gate, hidden tool predictions, the single logged look and chronology audits meant that the central results could be checked after the fact (reviews/audit_order_M9.md).
  • Independent re-derivation caught the 401/820 tie problem and the 646/635 expressed-gene definition gap.
  • Pre-written branches turned disappointing results into reported ones. No gene in a tier and GLS parity were stated plainly, not worked around.
  • Role-specific referees found the problems every earlier check missed. These were all definition or denominator issues ("per what?"): the conditional p_cal, the null-inflated census, the definition artefact and the missing novelty baseline (reviews/retro_M9.md §3).

Where it went in circles.

  • Design review produced many small fixes and missed the big ones. Two review rounds and two disposition checks found 7 and then 32 gaps, all fixed within about an hour. They did not catch the conditional meaning of p_cal or the route by which complex subunits entered the list. Both were found only at manuscript review.
  • Operational details left open at the freeze (tie-breaks, fill order, file definitions, bootstrap mechanics) generated 22 post-freeze deviation entries. About 13 of them filled details the design had not specified, and some were committed together with the results they governed (see DISCREPANCIES.md).
  • Unvalidated checks decided nothing. The top-40 robustness checks consumed a 55-minute run and an iterative fill procedure, failed 221/269 genes, and ended as labels. The orthogonal-evidence rule (32% vs 28% vs 22%) could not rank predictions either.
  • Novelty was assessed late. Ten reports were written, red-teamed and revised (about 300 cited spans checked, none fabricated) before anyone checked earlier catalogues. Nine then needed novelty corrections.

Where human input changed direction. It did not. Every change of direction came from agents: the literature review (definition, temporal hold-out), round-1 reviewers (assessability null, ranker options, circularity), the independent verifier (ties), the PI (fill rule, strong-signal list) and the manuscript referees (reframing).

Full tables: DEVIATIONS.md, results/revision/SUMMARY.md, manuscript/supplementary/.

Key insights

The main point: for the biologist, most genes that databases call "uncharacterised" are either invisible to cancer-cell CRISPR screens or already have a published function. Where co-essentiality does say something, it is specific but rarely the exact answer, and simple homology does far better. For the methodologist, every number that looked encouraging shrank once someone asked what it was conditional on, or applied the negative control's error rate back to it.

A ranked half-page summary comes first. Below it, insights are grouped and ranked within each group by how general and how surprising they are. Each links to where it arose. "Shown" means measured in this project; "believed" means a likely explanation that was not tested. Insight labels (Bio-, Meth-, Eng-) are not the project's milestone (M1–M9) or referee-item (M1, S1…) names. Terms are defined in JOURNEY.md and the METHOD.md glossary.

The insights in half a page

Ranked by how much they should change what a reader does. Details and sources follow below.

For biologists

  1. Co-essentiality rarely names the exact function, and homology does far better. On 809 genes annotated after 2018, its top GO term was right for 3.0%, against 21.8% for the gene's own electronic/phylogenetic annotations (Bio-1).
  2. "Uncharacterised" in databases often means "uncurated". 42% of a random 50 already had a published function (Bio-2).
  3. Most uncharacterised genes are invisible to CRISPR co-essentiality. 646 of 4,924 (13%) pass the usable-signal rule; at least ~322 (6.5%) carry real signal (Bio-3).
  4. The most confident calls are mostly rediscoveries. 18/40 top predictions were literature-supported, but 31/40 genes already had a published function and 34/40 had a prior catalogue link (Bio-4).

For methodologists

  1. Leave-one-out flatters. Accuracy on known genes was about five times that on genes annotated after 2018 (13.9% vs 3.0%) (Meth-1).
  2. A hold-out of later-annotated genes gives conditional probabilities. Expected confirmations fell from 30.5 to about 4.9 once this was accounted for (Meth-2).
  3. Apply the negative control's error rate back to every count. About 400 of 646 "usable signal" calls were expected under the null (Meth-3).
  4. Benchmark against the annotation the database already has. The homology baseline beat co-essentiality sevenfold (Meth-4).

1. Scientific and domain insights

Bio-1. On genuinely new annotations, co-essentiality is specific but weak, and homology is far stronger. Shown. For 809 genes annotated after 2018, the top predicted GO term was right for 3.0%, against 0.5% for matched genes. Ranking the gene's own 2018 electronic/phylogenetic terms gave 21.8%. The signal sits in the strongest-dependency fifth of genes (11.7%) and in complex membership (18.2%). It is complementary: 15 of its 24 hits were missed by homology. As a fallback where homology is silent, it adds +0.6 points (21.8% → 22.4%). → TP5.

Bio-2. "Uncharacterised" in databases often means "uncurated", not "unknown". Shown. In a random 50 of 4,924 genes with no experimental GO process/function annotation and low annotation or literature counts, 42% (29–56%) already had an experimentally established function. The rate was 56% for genes that entered through the literature-attention route (few focused papers or IDG Tdark) without a low UniProt score, against 13% for genes with a low UniProt annotation score. Believed: counting only papers about ≤ 10 genes misses complex subunits characterised in multi-subunit papers (288 of the genes are Complex Portal subunits). This extends the knownness critiques of Stoeger 2018 (doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.2006643) and Haynes 2018 (doi:10.1038/s41598-018-19333-x) to the definitions used in function-prediction studies. → TP1, TP8.

Bio-3. Most uncharacterised genes carry no co-essentiality information. Shown. 646 of 4,924 (13%) passed the reproducibility-plus-expression rule. Non-expressed control genes passed the reproducibility test at 13% (27% with any dependency), so the 646 assessable calls exceed the null expectation by only about 241. Under an untested assumption, at least about 322 genes (6.5%) carry real signal. The pipeline still writes flagged predictions for the others, and about 82% of the summed calibrated probability comes from them (derived for this explainer). Chemosensory/epidermal family genes: 2 of 516. → TP3.

Bio-4. The most confident co-essentiality calls are mostly rediscoveries. Shown. Blinded judges supported 18 of the top 40 predictions against 3/120 decoys, but 31 of the 40 genes already had published function. 34/40 had a link with a top partner in earlier catalogues, and 9 of 10 deep-dive genes had a published co-essential relationship (3 were explicit Wainberg 2021 predictions, doi:10.1038/s41588-021-00840-z). Of the ten deep-dive genes, only PLEKHH3 (a co-advantage partner of PTEN and PLEKHA1) had no prior; 6 of the top 40 had no prior in any resource checked. → TP7, TP8.

Bio-5. A better co-complex score did not give better function predictions. Shown. zavg_BEF leads GLS by +0.10 in average precision (AP) on the tool's co-complex benchmark, but on the hold-out it tied GLS (+0.006, CI −0.005 to +0.017) and Pearson (+0.002). Believed: the bottleneck is GO-term assignment and the scarcity of strongly dependent new genes, not pair scoring. → TP5.

Bio-6. DepMap-derived annotations are rare in GO overall but concentrated in the famous success stories. Shown. Only 1.8% of hold-out targets cite a paper that used DepMap, and removing them moved precision@1 from 0.032 to 0.030. But they were most of the targets of SLC25A51 (18/19), FIRRM (14/15) and CCDC32 (4/5), so these stories cannot serve as independent validation. → TP2.

Bio-7. Where co-essentiality is strongest, it cannot be calibrated. Shown. Mitochondrial, DNA-repair, ribosome, nuclear-RNA and centrosome terms each had fewer than 30 hold-out genes, and the strongest signals lay beyond the hold-out's range. These predictions therefore got no calibrated probability. The uncalibrated top 20 from these families were supported 19/20 by judges, but all 20 had earlier catalogue links. At the other end, signalling/lineage terms were right for 0 of 111 hold-out genes. This fits the mitochondrial dominance of co-essentiality signal reported by Rahman 2021 (doi:10.15252/msb.202010013). → TP6.

2. Methodological insights

These generalise to other guilt-by-association or function-prediction studies.

Meth-1. Leave-one-out accuracy was about five times the accuracy on newly annotated genes. Shown. The same predictor scored precision@1 0.139 on 2,519 known genes with their own annotations hidden, and 0.030 on genes annotated after 2018. A calibration fitted on the known genes predicted 0.089 on the hold-out, where 0.031 was observed. Believed: part of the gap is that known genes are more essential and better connected (standardised differences of 0.1–0.5 between the two gene sets), as the multifunctionality argument of Gillis & Pavlidis predicts (2011, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0017258; 2012, doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002444). The CAFA-style temporal hold-out (Radivojac 2013, doi:10.1038/nmeth.2340) is the test that matters. → TP2, TP5.

Meth-2. A hold-out built from genes that later got annotated yields conditional probabilities. Shown. Calibrating on such genes estimates P(correct | the gene is annotated later). Only 16% of eligible 2018 genes gained annotation, so the expected number of confirmed predictions fell from 30.5 to about 4.9 once this was accounted for. Any CAFA-style calibration should state its conditioning. → TP8.

Meth-3. Apply the negative control's false-call rate back to every count. Shown. The split-half reproducibility test was nominally a 5% test but passed 13–27% of non-expressed control genes. Counting assessable genes without subtracting expected false calls hid that about 400 of the 646 calls were expected under the null alone. → TP3.

Meth-4. Benchmark against the annotation the database already has. Shown. The trivial "homology" baseline (rank the gene's own electronic and phylogenetic GO terms at the start date) beat co-essentiality sevenfold on the hold-out. Believed: curators often confirm experimentally what electronic annotation already suggested, so this baseline is hard to beat for any new-function predictor. → TP5.

Meth-5. Fix the novelty baseline before choosing candidates. Shown. A blind literature screen judged novelty from papers. Only after ten reports were written did a check against earlier co-essentiality catalogues show that 9 of the 10 genes had a published co-essential link. → TP8.

Meth-6. Decoys and a known-gene validation set turn literature support into a test, but the scoring rule is part of the endpoint. Shown. Three decoys per gene gave an interpretable false-support rate (3/120), and judge validation (9/10 vs 1/30) showed the judges could discriminate. A rule crediting module-label matches existed only in the judge prompt. It changed the headline from 16/40 to 18/40, and it helped only real statements, because every supported decoy was supported on its term. Agreement between two instances of one model (κ 0.975) is not validity. → TP7.

Meth-7. Validate a check on known positives and decoys before it can promote or demote. Shown. Robustness checks failed 221 of 269 candidates. The orthogonal-evidence rule supported 32% of real, 28% of matched-gene and 22% of decoy predictions. Neither had been tried on known positives first, and neither ended up deciding anything. → TP6, appendix.

Meth-9. A ranking from a thin calibration is fragile. Shown. The calibration rested on 24 correct calls. Simpler post-review models were equally well calibrated but shared only 7–14 of the top 40 genes with the frozen model. Report the expected count, not a ranked list, as the primary output. → TP8.

3. Lower-ranked observations

True and measured, but narrower or less actionable than the ones above.

Bio-8. CRISPR co-dependencies of candidate genes rarely replicate in RNAi. Shown, with a caveat. For 182 of 204 measured candidates, the mean correlation with their CRISPR partners in DEMETER2 RNAi data was not above the 95th percentile of random partner sets. Believed: this reflects RNAi noise and partial knockdown as much as CRISPR artefacts; the check was never run on known positives, so it cannot separate the two. → TP6.

Meth-8. Set thresholds and power assumptions from the achievable range. Shown. Tiers required p_cal ≥ 0.5 or 0.3 when the base rate was 3% and the maximum p_cal was 0.141. The power simulation assumed null precision of 0.05–0.15, where 0.000–0.005 was observed. A dry run of the scoring and calibration on known genes before the freeze would have shown both. → TP6.

Meth-10. The simplest ranker can win and still need guarding. Shown. A summed neighbour score beat hypergeometric and matched-gene p-values by a pre-declared rule (MRR 0.169 vs 0.140 vs 0.111). But its top terms were broad (median 131 genes), and its top score was tied in 401/820 genes, mostly between a term and its parent. Specify tie-breaks, and report the most specific term alongside. → TP4.

4. Engineering details for reproduction

Eng-1. Make "no look" rules mechanisms. The gene list and design are covered by preregistration/FREEZE.sha256; src/gate.py::gate.check() refuses pairwise computation unless the hash and tag match. The tool's precomputed predictions were hidden by sparse checkout (scripts/verify_sparse.sh), and scripts/audit_order.py checks that no pairwise output predates the tag (PASS at all three chronology audits: after the census, after the predictions and at the end). → TP1.

Eng-2. Git order is the only proof of "specified before". The hold-out specification preceded the look by 31 minutes. But several rows marked "set before computing" were committed in the same commit as, or after, the results they governed, so their order cannot be shown (see DISCREPANCIES.md). Commit specification files separately, before the run. → TP5.

Eng-3. Write an executable spec for every operational detail. 22 post-freeze deviation entries, about 13 of them filling unspecified details (tie-breaks, fill order, covariate release, TF list, bootstrap mechanics). See DEVIATIONS.md and reviews/retro_M7.md §3.

Eng-4. R1 tie-break = ascending GO id. Descending order changes 393 labels; precision@1 0.032 vs 0.030. → TP4.

Eng-5. Expressed-gene definition. The frozen list's expressed column predates the lineage-restricted clause in DESIGN §1.4, giving 635 vs 646 assessable genes. Both are reported. → TP3.

Eng-6. One implementation per definition. A 7-term vs 22-term "generic binding" GO list changed 17 genes in the uncharacterised list. The independent re-derivation found it, and the 22-term list in src/knownness.py is the frozen one (preregistration/PROVENANCE.md).

Eng-7. Cluster bootstrap fallback. Linking hold-out genes by shared papers or shared neighbours made one cluster of 63.5% of genes; the primary CIs use paper-only clusters (709 clusters; logged before the look) (results/holdout_eval/SUMMARY.md).

Eng-8. Circularity detection depends on full text. The Europe PMC query searched full text for 71.7% of supporting papers. No abstract-only paper was flagged, so circularity is a lower bound (results/holdout/circularity_summary.md).

Eng-9. IPI leakage rule. When scoring gene g, drop protein-interaction annotations (evidence IPI) whose "with/from" field names g. Otherwise a neighbour's annotation can encode the interaction with g itself (src/vocab.py).

Eng-10. Reproduce the tool before using it. zavg_BEF internal-test average precision (AP) 0.3451 vs published 0.345; GLS and Pearson rows match the tool to < 3e-7; 14/14 sign and orientation checks (results/verification/).

Eng-11. Literature agents need symbol hygiene. Searches must cover previous symbols and aliases and exclude collisions (for example STOML3 alias SRO, GPR152 alias PGR5). Catalogues from 2019 use old symbols: INAFM1 = PRR24, BICRAL = GLTSCR1L (docs/AGENT_PROMPTS.md).

Eng-12. Monotone demotions. Make demotions monotone in iterative fills (once demoted, never re-promoted when the set of genes over which Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control is applied changes), or the fill can cycle (DEVIATIONS.md).

Eng-13. Record keeping. Use git UTC times; agent-written dates in the record are inconsistent (some say 31 October). Enforce the agent-run log: results/agent_runs.tsv has 1 row. Checkpoint before long agent runs: the usage-limit stop left unreviewed edits (379827f).
